title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
purpose: It assembles transmitted testimony from the Imams and Ismaili masters on the ranks of the Imams and their subordinate hudud, and on the duties, prohibitions and limits binding those loyal to them.

points.text: Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen, in the book of the Esoteric Nursing, interprets the Quranic verse 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' as referring to the Imams among God's servants.

On the same authority, 'those who were made weak in the land' whom God will make Imams and heirs means the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, weakened in the person of Ali himself, who is the proof of Muhammad and whose likeness is the earth.

Al-Muizz li Din Allah, in his Sunday supplication, sets out a descending order of ranks: beneath the Foundation (al-Asas) the Terminus (al-Mutimm) facing Israfil, beneath the Terminus the After (al-Lahiq) facing Michael, and beneath the After the Wing (al-Janah) facing Gabriel.

Al-Muizz holds that these three (the Grandfather/al-Jadd, the Opener/al-Fath, and the Imagination/al-Khayal — i.e. Israfil, Michael, Gabriel) transmit to the respondents from the Speaker and the Foundation in the bodily world, just as three transmit from the two roots, the Pen and the Tablet, in the spiritual world.

In his Friday supplication al-Muizz enumerates seven hudud — the Speaker, the Foundation, the Terminus, the After, the Wing, the Authorized (al-Madhun) and the Respondent (al-Mustajib) — together with twelve proofs ranked across twelve regions, which the author correlates with the Quranic 'over it are nineteen'.

Ali ibn Abi Talib's supplication of victory and awe invokes numbered ranks — the six transmitted, the seven beheld, the nine signs, the ten words, the twenty-one, the eight who encircle the Throne, the eleven who prostrate and the twelve counted ones who bow.

In his Four Hundred Manners Ali names seven Imams, seven successors, seven witnesses and seven substitutes, and declares that whoever holds fast to them joins the truth while whoever holds to another way is undone.

Muhammad bin Tahir, in a supplication, seeks nearness to God through the Imams' gates, proofs, preachers, authorized ones, the respondents of their cycles, and all who incline toward, shelter in, follow or are guided by them.

Ali prohibits both exaggeration and falling short concerning the Imams: believers must say the Imams are servants under a Lord, though they may say whatever they wish of their excellence — and he adds that the exaggerator will return to them and they themselves will raise up the one who falls short.

Ali's commandment to those who love the Imams requires doing their work with God-fearing restraint, not sitting with those who revile them, and not praising them openly before the enemy — so that love of them be plain and hatred of them concealed — together with truthfulness, patience, and not burdening the Imams with intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

Further maxims from the Four Hundred Manners: beware disputation, for it bequeaths doubt; reckon speech as part of deeds; hasten to good works and let most speech be remembrance of God; sins withhold provision; the best deed of the believer is awaiting the relief; and blessed is he admonished by another's case.

The nineteenth of the Mustansiriya councils teaches that the kinship God commands to be joined contains a seven and a twelve, the seven being the Imams of the religion indicated by 'I ask you no reward except affection toward my kin', recurring like the days of Friday.
